what: Differential reduction through opposing gear ratios. One motor drives two real gear paths into a differential. One side follows the input at +1; the other turns oppositely at -27/25. The differential carrier follows their signed mean, -1/25. A separate equal gear pair reverses that slow motion, so the visible passive output pointer makes one positive turn for every 25 input turns. The finite experiment pauses at quarter turns, completes one output revolution, reverses and returns home. These ratios are geometric predictions; the packaged acceptance record separately reports what the exported model and program actually demonstrated. try: In Robot Lab choose File → Open a model… and select models/vernier-drive.ldr. Choose Mat → Plain. In Code select Pseudocode, paste all of programs/vernier-drive.bw and choose ⇦ To blocks. Use Reset to restore the saved pose and encoder datum, then press Robot Lab Run. This isolated add-on is not automatically installed in Examples.

Stages 0–4 visit output pointer angles 0°, 90°, 180°, 270° and 360°. Stages 5–8 return through 270°, 180°, 90° and 0°. Each measured motor arrival has a one-second teaching dwell. A completed run ends with completed = 1, failed = 0, stage = 9 and arrived = 0; the input motor holds the attained home position.

At the 90° output pause, the ideal input and left side have turned +6.25 revolutions, the right side -6.75, and the differential carrier -0.25. Their signed mean is (-0.5)/2 = -0.25 turn. The external equal gear pair reverses that carrier motion to +0.25 turn at the output pointer.

At 360°, compare the actual unwrapped rotations: +25 input turns, +25 left-side turns, -27 right-side turns, -1 carrier turn and +1 output turn. A pointer that returns to the same visible direction after one turn still traveled through a complete revolution. Use continuously unwrapped actual body angles rather than just start/end orientations or requested targets.

The displayed outputTarget refers to the separate visible pointer, not the differential carrier. The motor target is 25 times the output angle, with the measured encoder sign: 9000 motor degrees for one output turn. The nominal command of 240 motor degrees per second corresponds to 9.6 output degrees per second between pauses. Reset before a fresh run after any manual movement or interrupted experiment.
why: An external gear mesh reverses direction and multiplies rotation by the driver tooth count divided by the driven tooth count. The three-mesh branch therefore gives -(12/20) × (12/20) × (36/12) = -27/25 relative to the common input. The other side is driven directly at +1. Equal differential side gears obey C = (L + R)/2, so C = (1 - 27/25)I/2 = -I/25. The separate 16-tooth to 16-tooth output mesh reverses the sign once more: O = -C = I/25. The small output comes from the difference between two larger opposite motions. All signed angles must use a consistent physical axis convention; the positions of opposed shafts on the screen do not determine the signs.
matters: A large reduction can emerge by combining nearly opposing motions, even though neither side path is a large reduction by itself. Here the fast branches differ by two turns after 25 input turns, and the differential halves that difference. Mean Machine already demonstrates a differential averaging two independently commanded motors; this experiment uses one input and real tooth ratios to generate the near cancellation mechanically. It establishes rotational kinematics, not torque multiplication, efficiency, self-locking, backlash, wear or a physical load rating.
question: After the input makes 25 positive turns, the sides make +25 and -27 turns. Does their difference make the carrier turn twice, once, or not at all? What does the visible output pointer do?
answer: The carrier turns once in the negative direction because the differential takes the signed mean: (25 - 27)/2 = -1. The separate equal external gear pair reverses that motion, so the visible output pointer turns once positively. If the side ratios were exactly +1 and -1, their mean would be zero; a large ratio by near cancellation depends on the small remaining difference.
further: Predict the left, right, carrier and output rotations after 12.5 input turns. Then compare those predictions with independently observed body-carried markers at the 180° output pause.
Test the mean relation C = (L + R)/2 using measured left and right angles, separately from testing O = I/25. A correct-looking output alone does not show that both intended side paths are working.

Compare matching forward and reverse phases. The ideal ratio is unchanged. Any discrepancy in a measured run needs investigation; this simulation is not a measurement of real LEGO backlash or friction.

Trace each physical mesh and count its teeth. Explain why the three-mesh branch changes sign three times and why the final 16:16 mesh changes only direction. Inspect the collars and bearing supports that retain the fast shafts throughout their full rotations.
formula: I = actual common input angle; L = I; R = -(12/20)(12/20)(36/12)I = -(27/25)I; C = (L + R)/2 = -I/25; O = -C = I/25. At I = 25 turns: L = +25, R = -27, C = -1, O = +1 turn. outputTarget is O in degrees. Native motor encoder sign is measured separately; actual input, both sides, carrier and output body angles are observed independently of the command.
